claims.text: The starting composite consists of discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite displays phase separation under service conditions.
The untreated W–Cu composite forms voids at W–Cu interfaces under service conditions.
A thin Ni coating can be deposited on reinforcement particles before spark-plasma-sintering consolidation using a physical-vapor-deposition-type process.
Pre-coating the W phase with Ni will suppress phase separation in W–Cu.
Pre-coating the W phase with Ni will suppress interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
A deposited Ni-containing interlayer can improve interfacial bonding in a consolidated composite.
A Ni interlayer improves the wettability of W by Cu.
A Ni interlayer enhances interdiffusion across the W–Cu interface during consolidation.
Improved wettability and interdiffusion prevent W–Cu phase separation during subsequent thermal and irradiation stresses.
Improved wettability and interdiffusion prevent W–Cu interfacial void formation during subsequent thermal and irradiation stresses.
Reducing phase separation and interfacial voids will increase the thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically processed uncoated composite.
The predicted improvement applies under high heat flux, thermal cycling, and irradiation relevant to plasma-facing W/Cu joints.
Coating uniformity, coating thickness, and processing parameters may affect the magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement.
Coated and uncoated W–Cu samples should be manufactured under identical processing conditions and compared after the same heat-flux cycling and irradiation exposure.
Interfacial void fraction and phase separation can be compared using high-resolution electron microscopy.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant void reduction and a corresponding thermal-conductivity increase would falsify the hypothesis.
